reports.name: Shohei Ohtani
reports.published_report: The Statcast batting profile is almost uniformly elite: .407 xwOBA, .569 xSLG, 93.3 mph average exit velocity, a 16.4% barrel rate, all sitting in the 96th-to-98th percentile range. The one legitimate crack is a 30.5% whiff rate that lands in just the 18th percentile, and a 23.0% strikeout rate that trails the contact profile by a wide margin, meaning the bat-to-ball side is the ceiling cap on what the underlying quality deserves. On the mound, a 2.72 xERA and 30.4% whiff rate against hitters point to a starter who misses real bats, and the 3.8% barrel rate allowed signals that when contact comes, it's mostly soft, though the 7.6% walk rate is the one thing that can quietly unravel an outing. The projection asks for .287/.392/.548 with 38 home runs across 693 plate appearances, which is what this Statcast profile earns if the strikeout rate doesn't drift further upward and if the elbow holds across a full two-way workload back in Los Angeles.

reports.name: James Wood
reports.published_report: The contact-and-power profile here is as loud as it gets: a 20.8% barrel rate and a 95.1 mph average exit velocity both sitting at the 100th percentile, with an xSLG of .585 that says the projection's .523 SLG is conservative. Wood also runs a 16.8% walk rate that almost no hitter at this level can match. The whole thing hinges on whether a 28.6% strikeout rate, bottom 12% of the league, ever comes down, because at the current whiff rate the gap between what he should hit and what he actually hits stays wide. If it does compress even modestly, you're talking about a legitimate MVP-caliber season out of a 23-year-old; if it doesn't, the .387 OBP and the power still make him a middle-of-the-order force, just a noisier one.

reports.name: Sal Stewart
reports.published_report: Thirty-four projected home runs from a 22-year-old corner infielder would be notable at any age, but what makes Stewart's power believable is a 14.0% barrel rate that grades in the 89th percentile, paired with an .xSLG of .468 that lines up almost exactly with the projected .472 SLG. The read on his Statcast card is essentially a barrel-heavy slugger whose hard-hit rate at 39.5% sits below average, meaning he does his damage in concentrated bursts rather than by routinely scorching the ball, and a 26.6% whiff rate that's a tick below average keeps the 22.1% strikeout rate from being a problem. The 10.3% walk rate is quietly real, and it's what lifts the profile from a pure pull-side thumper toward something more durable, projecting to a .803 OPS over 694 plate appearances. If the barrel rate softens, the .247 xBA says there isn't much contact volume underneath it to keep the line afloat.

If it works, he's a .300 hitter with 42 stolen bases whose 95th-percentile fielding and sprint speed make the whole thing play; if the speed or glove erodes, the .264 xwOBA is a bench bat's floor, not a regular's. The entire profile hinges on whether a guy who almost never barrels anything can sustain a batting average that keeps the rest of it honest.

reports.name: Willi Castro
reports.published_report: The chase rate is the problem. At 38.2%, Castro is expanding the zone at a rate that puts him near the bottom of the league, and a 30.7% whiff rate means pitchers have learned they don't need to throw him anything good. The .233 xBA tells the honest story; whatever batting average he's run in short stretches, the contact quality underneath it is thin, with an 87.7 mph average exit velocity that sits well below average. His 8.8% barrel rate is the one real asset in the contact profile, and the projection's .259/.330/.417 line at 552 PA leans on that rate holding while assuming the approach doesn't get any worse. The speed is genuine at 28.2 ft/s, and in Coors that .417 projected SLG can breathe, but if the chase rate climbs further he becomes a high-variance bench piece rather than the versatile regular Colorado is counting on.

A 94.1 mph average exit velocity and 20.6% barrel rate produce an xSLG of .505 and an xwOBA of .365, both sitting at the top of the league, while a 17.3% walk rate keeps the OBP viable even when the bat-to-ball fails him. If the whiff rate holds, the projection's .233 average is a real cost, and the question is whether 37 projected home runs and a .874 OPS on a White Sox roster is a treasure hiding in plain sight or a frustrating split verdict between two extreme skills that never fully resolve.

reports.name: Bryson Stott
reports.published_report: The contact profile is the whole argument. Stott's xBA sits at .273, 81st percentile, built on an 18.9% whiff rate that ranks in the 79th percentile, and that combination of bat-to-ball and plate coverage is what makes a .261 projected AVG feel honest rather than flattering. He's not a power hitter: a 6.6% barrel rate and 40.5% hard-hit rate explain why the projection lands at 11 home runs across 581 plate appearances, and a .412 projected SLG lines up almost exactly with his .413 xSLG. What elevates him from solid-average second baseman to genuinely useful regular is the rest of the profile, 28 projected stolen bases off 81st-percentile sprint speed, a 94th-percentile OAA grade at second base, and enough walks at 9.5% BB% to keep the .334 OBP from depending on BABIP luck. The entire thing hinges on the contact skill holding; if the whiff rate creeps up, the power margin is too thin to compensate, and he becomes a useful bench piece rather than an everyday contributor.

reports.name: Mickey Moniak
reports.published_report: The .533 projected SLG tells you what kind of player he is when he connects — and the 11.2% barrel rate shows the contact quality is there when it happens. The problem is everything upstream of contact: a 41.5% chase rate sits in the 4th percentile, which means pitchers can exploit him early in counts and make those barrels genuinely rare, a dynamic the .227 xBA lays bare. Coors Field inflates the counting stats enough that a .269/.310/.533 projection line looks like a productive everyday outfielder, but strip the park out and what you have is a pull-power bat with below-average plate discipline who lives and dies on whether pitchers make mistakes. If the contact finds grass at that rate, he's a useful corner piece; if the chase rate keeps pitchers comfortable working him away, the barrels dry up and the .310 OBP becomes the loudest number in the room.

reports.name: Luke Adams
reports.published_report: The discipline-power combination at AAA is legitimate: 33 walks against only 37 strikeouts in 261 plate appearances, with a .252 ISO that translates to .18 at the MLB level. That's a hitter making contact, taking pitches, and doing real damage when he connects. The BABIP sitting at .245 means the .252 average is running below what the underlying profile suggests, so the .401 OBP is carrying itself almost entirely on plate discipline rather than fortunate contact. The translation puts his walk rate above league average and his strikeout rate well below it, which at first base means everything hinges on whether the power holds against better velocity — if it does, he's a low-end everyday regular; if it doesn't, you're left with a patient, light-hitting first baseman who is a bench bat at best.

This is a legitimate everyday catcher with real offensive upside, full stop.

reports.name: Bryce Miller
reports.published_report: The xERA is 2.75 and the walk rate is 4.9%, and those two numbers are basically the whole argument. Miller suppresses contact at an elite level, a 30.8% hard-hit rate that ranks well inside the top tenth of the league, and his 36.2% chase rate explains how he does it without needing swing-and-miss volume — the 26.4% whiff rate is ordinary, but hitters are expanding the zone against him rather than waiting him out. The projection at 3.46 ERA over 126.4 innings is the responsible number, a fair discount for health and regression risk on a guy whose Statcast profile reads like a mid-rotation anchor who actually pitches like a frontline one. Everything here hinges on his ability to stay in the Seattle rotation; the stuff plays in any role, but the value evaporates fast if he can't hold a full workload.

Across AAA & AA in 2026, Genao is hitting .300/.401/.474 through 419 plate appearances, with 60 walks against just 68 strikeouts — a discipline profile that translates to an 11.5 BB% and a K% sitting below league average at the MLB level. The power is the open question: his .174 ISO in the minors translates to .141 at the MLB equivalent, a tick below average, which means if he doesn't add loft or pull-side juice, he becomes a shortstop who gets on base rather than one who damages you. If the hit tool holds and the walks travel, he grows into a low-end everyday regular; if the power translation stays thin, what's left is a bench bat who can still take a walk.

reports.name: Slade Cecconi

An 18.0% K% and 20.3% whiff rate leave almost no margin for error, because when hitters put the ball in play at a 40.0% hard-hit rate, a staff needs misses to survive and Cecconi isn't generating them. reports.name: Noah Cameron
reports.published_report: The xERA sits at 4.39 and the fastball averages 92.5 mph, which puts him near the bottom fifth of starters by velocity. What keeps him functional is a walk rate of 7.6% that grades better than most of the rotation, and a 25.7% whiff rate that's roughly league-average, meaning hitters make contact but don't always punish it badly. The 29.1% chase rate is the soft spot: he can't expand the zone reliably, so the whiffs he gets come mostly from pitches over the plate, which is a narrow margin when the fastball already plays short. If the command holds and he sequences well enough to keep barrels down from that 8.7% figure, he's a back-end starter logging innings on a young Royals club; if the fastball gets elevated or the chase rate dips further, he slides into a bulk-inning role pretty quickly.

reports.name: Spencer Jones
reports.published_report: The ISO is the loudest thing in this profile, and it has a translation problem. At AAA in 2026, Spencer Jones is posting a .284 ISO across 233 plate appearances, which renders to .192 against MLB pitching, real power, but paired with a strikeout rate that translates to 28.1% when the AAA average sits at 22.0%. The discipline is genuinely there, 31 walks against 72 strikeouts at AAA, and the 10.5% translated walk rate clears its MLB counterpart of 8.5%, so the question isn't whether he can take a pitch. It's whether the strikeout rate compresses enough at the highest level to let the power carry a lineup spot, and if it doesn't, the .358 BABIP propping that .273 average comes down and you're left with a bench bat who swings and misses too much to start every day.

reports.name: Brian Curley
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the whole case. Across AA & A+, Curley has issued just 24 walks in 91.7 innings, a 2.4 BB/9 that translates to 2.9 in MLB context, and the 107 strikeouts over those same innings hint at a guy who can miss bats when he needs to. The translation doesn't flatter him everywhere, though: his K/9 softens to 8.2 in MLB equivalent, just a tick below the majors, and his K-BB% lands at 13.3% where the MLB average sits at 13.5%, leaving almost no margin. If the stuff thins against better contact, the command advantage carrying his profile right now may not be enough on its own. The ceiling is a back-end starter, and if the strikeout rate doesn't hold up a level, you're looking at a reliever who walks almost nobody — useful, not a rotation piece.

reports.name: Drew Beam
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the one thing working in his favor, and it isn't working hard enough. Across 95.7 innings at AA, Drew Beam has posted a 7.0 ERA with 74 strikeouts, and when his control translates to an MLB-equivalent context, his 3.2 BB/9 lands exactly at the MLB mean while his strikeout rate comes in at 6.7, well short of the 8.6 MLB average. That gap is the whole problem: a pitcher who doesn't miss bats has to live on sequencing and soft contact, and the 7.0 ERA at AA says that formula isn't holding. If something generates more swing-and-miss, there's a back-end starter conversation to be had; if the current shape holds, he's a depth arm.

reports.published_report: Low-end everyday regular ceiling, but the current damage points to a low-impact bench floor; he rarely gives pitchers an easy plate appearance. Pitchers do not have to change their plan for his power; the sample covers 394 PA in Single-A, so confidence is low.

reports.name: Gavin Conticello
reports.published_report: The sample covers 381 PA in Triple-A and Double-A, so confidence is high. He controls at-bats and does damage without leaning on one result. No single result is loud enough to carry the bat through regression elsewhere. The current-performance ceiling scenario is a low-end everyday regular who contributes across categories, with a useful bench-bat floor.
